name: keras
title: Keras: A Multi-Backend Deep Learning Framework for AI
answer: Keras is an open-source Python deep learning framework, now at version 3, that lets you build and train neural networks on top of JAX, TensorFlow, PyTorch, or OpenVINO. It sits at the model-building layer of the AI stack, offering a high-level API for layers, losses, optimizers, and training loops. The one thing to know before adopting it is that Keras 3 is a rewrite: existing tf.keras code using only built-in layers can run on other backends, but custom components must use keras.ops to stay portable.

sections.body: Keras is a Python library for deep learning, maintained by the Keras team and released under the Apache 2.0 licence. Its official site describes it as "Deep Learning for humans," and the repository has over 64,000 stars. It first appeared as a high-level interface for TensorFlow, and Keras 3.0, announced on the official site, turns it into a multi-backend framework. It occupies the model-definition and training layer of the AI stack: above numerical backends such as JAX, TensorFlow, and PyTorch, and below application code. It provides layers, models, metrics, losses, optimizers, callbacks, and training and evaluation loops, so you describe a network and train it without writing backend-specific code.
sections.heading: What it is and where it sits in AI work

sections.body: Keras handles the concrete jobs of training, evaluation, and inference. The official guides show image classification with MNIST, autoencoders built with the functional API, transfer learning for flower classification, and text generation with a mini-GPT model built using KerasHub. It supports data parallelism and model parallelism through the keras.distribution namespace, currently implemented for the JAX backend. It is strongest when you want a readable, consistent API across backends, when you need to move a model between JAX, TensorFlow, and PyTorch without rewriting it, and when you want built-in training loops that accept NumPy arrays, tf.data.Dataset objects, PyTorch DataLoader objects, and Pandas dataframes. The official site does not claim it is the fastest option for every model; it notes that JAX typically delivers the best performance in benchmarks, but results vary.
sections.heading: What it is used for and where it is strongest

sections.body: Keras is designed to be approachable. The Sequential guide starts with a plain stack of layers, and the functional API guide builds up to models with multiple inputs and outputs. You need basic Python and some familiarity with tensors and neural network concepts such as layers, loss functions, and optimizers. The official site offers guides, examples, and API documentation, including complete runnable scripts for MNIST and other datasets. The learning curve steepens when you write custom layers or losses, because Keras 3 requires using keras.ops rather than backend-specific operations if you want the code to work across JAX, PyTorch, and TensorFlow. The site does not state formal mathematics prerequisites, but the examples assume comfort with shapes, batches, and training loops.
sections.heading: How hard it is to learn and what you need first

sections.body: Keras has a broad ecosystem. The official site documents over a hundred layers, dozens of metrics, loss functions, optimizers, callbacks, and saving and serialization infrastructure. KerasHub provides pretrained models and layers, such as the TransformerDecoder used in the mini-GPT example. The keras.ops namespace offers cross-backend operations including matmul, sum, stack, einsum, softmax, binary_crossentropy, and conv. Integrations include tf.data.Dataset, PyTorch DataLoader, NumPy arrays, and Pandas dataframes. The project is hosted on GitHub under keras-team/keras, with an active repository and official documentation at keras.io. The site reports that Keras has been chosen by over 2.5 million developers and powers systems such as the Waymo self-driving fleet and the YouTube recommendation engine.
sections.heading: Ecosystem and community

sections.body: Keras is built for both quick experiments and production use, though the balance depends on the backend. The Sequential and functional APIs let you define and train a model in a few lines, and the built-in fit() and evaluate() loops handle batching, validation splits, and metrics. For production, Keras 3 lets a model be instantiated as a PyTorch Module, exported as a TensorFlow SavedModel, or instantiated as a stateless JAX function. The distribution API supports model and data parallelism, currently on JAX. The cost is that portability depends on discipline: custom layers must use keras.ops, and the site notes that the distribution API is not yet available for the TensorFlow and PyTorch backends. Performance varies by model, so benchmarking on your own workload is necessary.
sections.heading: Prototyping speed against production performance

sections.body: Keras is a current standard rather than a legacy choice. The official site states it has been chosen by over 2.5 million developers and is used in systems such as the Waymo self-driving fleet and the YouTube recommendation engine. Keras 3 is a recent release that extends the framework to JAX, TensorFlow, PyTorch, and OpenVINO for inference. For someone choosing what to learn, Keras offers a transferable skill: models built with built-in layers can run across backends, and existing tf.keras models using built-in layers can start running in JAX and PyTorch right away. The site does not provide a breakdown of job roles or hiring demand, so claims about career outcomes beyond adoption figures are not supported by the official material.
sections.heading: Industry adoption and careers

sections.body: Keras is typically used with Python and sits alongside JAX, TensorFlow, and PyTorch rather than replacing them. In the polyglot pattern, Keras is the high-level model-building language, and the backend is the execution engine. A Keras model can be instantiated as a PyTorch Module, exported as a TensorFlow SavedModel, or instantiated as a stateless JAX function. The keras.ops namespace provides a common set of operations so custom components can work across backends. The official site also mentions OpenVINO for inference-only workflows. This means a team can prototype in one backend and deploy in another, provided the model uses built-in layers or keras.ops throughout.
sections.heading: How it fits beside the others

sections.body: Keras is not the best fit for every situation. The Sequential model is explicitly not appropriate for non-linear topology such as residual connections or multi-branch models, and the functional API is the recommended alternative. The distribution API is currently implemented only for the JAX backend, with the TensorFlow and PyTorch backends described as coming soon. Performance is backend-dependent, and the site notes that non-XLA TensorFlow is occasionally faster on GPU than JAX. The official material does not state minimum hardware requirements, does not provide a detailed comparison against every competing framework, and does not say when the distribution API will reach the other backends. Those questions remain open in the pages reviewed.
sections.heading: Limits and open questions
